set1.q: Why is Pseudomonas aeruginosa a frequent contaminant of ventilators, intravenous solutions and anesthesia equipment?
opts: It forms endospores
Pseudomonas forms no spores; it persists on equipment by producing biofilms, and it resists soaps, disinfectants and drying.
It needs rich nutrients
It survives in nutrient-poor environments rather than needing rich ones; on equipment it persists by forming biofilms.
It lives inside amebas
Living in close association with amebas is how Legionella persists in water systems; Pseudomonas aeruginosa contaminates equipment by producing biofilms.

Correct: its ability to produce biofilms lets it contaminate ventilators, intravenous solutions and anesthesia equipment; cells in biofilms adhere by flagella and pili and form microcolonies.

opts: Fluid and electrolyte secretion

Booster doses for children and adolescents answer waning pertussis immunity; plague is prevented by quarantine and rodent control.
Pasteurizing dairy products
Avoiding unpasteurized dairy prevents brucellosis; plague is prevented by quarantine and rodent control.
Quarantine and rodent control

Correct: plague is prevented by quarantine and control of the rodent population in human habitats; a killed or attenuated vaccine is available for military personnel, veterinarians and laboratory workers.

set1.q: In the scheme for Gram-negative pathogens, which genus is the obligate anaerobe?
opts: Escherichia
Escherichia is a facultative anaerobe that ferments lactose; the obligate anaerobe in the scheme is Bacteroides.
Haemophilus
Haemophilus is a facultative anaerobe on the non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-positive branch; the obligate anaerobe is Bacteroides.
Bacteroides
Correct: the obligate anaerobes branch of the Gram-negative rods holds Bacteroides; the aerobes include Pseudomonas, and the facultative anaerobes include Escherichia and Haemophilus.
Pseudomonas
Pseudomonas is on the aerobic branch, the rods that do not ferment carbohydrates; the obligate anaerobe in the scheme is Bacteroides.

set2.q: How is Shigella transmitted?
opts: By animal bites and scratches
Animal bites and scratches spread Pasteurella multocida; Shigella is transmitted by eating fecally contaminated food.
By swallowing contaminated food
Correct: Shigella is transmitted by ingestion of fecally contaminated food; it then invades the villi of the large intestine.
By inhaling contaminated aerosols
Aerosols spread Legionella, pertussis and pneumonic plague; Shigella is swallowed in fecally contaminated food.
By the bite of an infected flea
Flea bites spread plague; Shigella is transmitted by ingestion of fecally contaminated food.

set2.q: Why is pertussis incidence highest among babies under 1 year old?
opts: They receive a whole-cell vaccine
Infants are given the acellular DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis) series, not a whole-cell vaccine; the highest incidence is in infants too young (under 2 months) to vaccinate.
They are too young to be vaccinated
Correct: average incidence is highest among children under 1 year because infants less than 2 months old cannot get vaccinated.
They are the main healthy carriers
The reservoir is apparently healthy carriers in general, not infants in particular; infants suffer most because the youngest cannot yet be vaccinated.

set2.q: In chronic Gram-negative infections, how have some bacteria adapted to evade the immune system?
opts: By altering their lipopolysaccharide
Correct: in chronic Gram-negative infections, some bacteria have adapted by modifying their lipopolysaccharide to evade the immune system.
By forming endospores
These bacilli are non-spore-forming; the adaptation described for chronic infection is a modified lipopolysaccharide.
By shedding their outer membrane
The outer membrane holds the lipopolysaccharide and is kept; the adaptation is to modify the lipopolysaccharide itself.

set2.q: The diagram shows enteric bacteria invading the intestinal epithelium, with bleeding. Which organism is the example of this invasive diarrheal disease?
opts: Klebsiella pneumoniae

Proteus vulgaris

Correct: invasive diarrheal disease, with bacteria entering the epithelium and causing bleeding, is exemplified by Shigella; the toxigenic pattern, an oversecretion of fluid, by enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli.
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli is the example of TOXIGENIC disease, an oversecretion of fluid without invasion; the invasive example is Shigella.

Melioidosis is Burkholderia pseudomallei infection from tropical soil and water; enteroinvasive Escherichia coli resembles shigellosis.

Correct: enteroinvasive Escherichia coli causes an inflammatory disease of the large intestine similar to shigellosis, with profuse bloody diarrhea and high fever.

Typhoid fever is Salmonella typhi's invasive disease of the small intestine leading to septicemia; enteroinvasive Escherichia coli resembles shigellosis.

set2.q: Which disease was Haemophilus influenzae once mistakenly thought to cause?
opts: Whooping cough
Whooping cough is pertussis, caused by Bordetella pertussis; Haemophilus influenzae was misnamed as the cause of the flu.
Pink eye
Pink eye (acute conjunctivitis) is caused by Haemophilus aegyptius; Haemophilus influenzae was misnamed as the cause of the flu.
Chancroid
Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; Haemophilus influenzae was misnamed as the cause of the flu.
Influenza (the flu)
Correct: Haemophilus influenzae was misnamed as the causative agent of the flu; it causes acute bacterial meningitis, epiglottitis, otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia and bronchitis.

set2.q: How does enteropathogenic Escherichia coli damage the intestine?
opts: Adheres and destroys microvilli
Correct: the bacteria adhere to the intestinal lining and destroy the microvilli; they also inhibit the uptake of vitamin B1 (thiamin).
Invades the villi of the colon
Invading the villi of the large intestine is what Shigella does; enteropathogenic Escherichia coli adheres to the lining and destroys microvilli.
Secretes heat-stable toxin
The heat-stable and heat-labile toxins belong to enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli; the enteropathogenic strain adheres and destroys microvilli.
Releases Shiga toxin into vessels
Shiga toxin damaging the endothelium is the enterohemorrhagic mechanism; enteropathogenic Escherichia coli adheres and destroys microvilli.

set2.q: The colonies on this plate have stained the agar greenish-blue. Which organism makes this pigment?
opts: Proteus vulgaris
Proteus vulgaris is recognized by its wavelike swarming growth, not a pigment; greenish-blue agar points to Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Correct: the greenish-blue color spreading through the agar is pyocyanin, the pigment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa; many pseudomonads make water-soluble pigments.
Serratia marcescens
Serratia marcescens makes a red pigment, prodigiosin, rather than a greenish-blue one; that pigment belongs to Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Klebsiella pneumoniae is recognized by its large capsule, not a pigment; the greenish-blue pigment is Pseudomonas aeruginosa's pyocyanin.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which three properties are used to differentiate the Gram-negative bacilli?
opts: Spores, acid-fastness and capsule
These Gram-negative bacilli are non-spore-forming, and acid-fastness is not on the list; they are sorted by oxygen requirement, lactose fermentation and oxidase.
Catalase, coagulase and hemolysis
None of these three is a sorting property here (all enterics are catalase positive); the three are oxygen requirement, lactose fermentation and oxidase.
Shape, size and pigment
Pigment marks some species, such as the greenish-blue of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, but is not a sorting axis; the three are oxygen, lactose fermentation and oxidase.
Oxygen, lactose and oxidase
Correct: Gram-negative bacilli are differentiated by oxygen requirements (aerobic, facultatively anaerobic, obligate anaerobic), the ability to ferment lactose, and the oxidase enzyme.

Haemophilus are tiny pleomorphic Gram-negative rods but are not described with bipolar staining; that is Yersinia pestis.

set2.q: Which opportunist survives for months on fomites and infects traumatic wounds such as combat injuries?
opts: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
Stenotrophomonas maltophilia forms biofilms that contaminate disinfectants and medical equipment; months on fomites and combat wounds describe Acinetobacter baumannii.
Brucella suis
Brucella suis is the pig species of brucellosis, caught from animals; the fomite survivor of combat wounds is Acinetobacter baumannii.
Acinetobacter baumannii

Correct: Acinetobacter baumannii causes nosocomial and community-acquired infections, survives months on fomites, and infects wounds, lungs, the urinary tract, burns and blood, including after traumatic combat wounds.
Burkholderia cepacia
Burkholderia cepacia is a rapidly mutating opportunist that troubles cystic fibrosis patients; months on fomites and combat wounds describe Acinetobacter baumannii.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Who are the hosts of Salmonella typhi?
opts: Humans exclusively
Correct: humans are the exclusive hosts of Salmonella typhi and Salmonella paratyphi, the most serious pathogens of the genus, causing typhoid and paratyphoid fever.
Poultry and their eggs
Poultry and eggs carry the animal salmonelloses such as Salmonella enteritidis; Salmonella typhi infects humans only.
Reptiles such as turtles
Pet turtles and bearded dragons spread the animal salmonelloses; the hosts of Salmonella typhi are humans exclusively.
Cattle and dairy herds
Cattle and dairy products carry animal salmonelloses (and Escherichia coli O157:H7); Salmonella typhi's hosts are humans exclusively.
set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 73, 60, 76 and 77

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: What makes a plague-infected flea ravenous?
opts: Murine toxin paralyzes its gut
Murine toxin is listed among the virulence factors, but the flea's hunger comes from coagulase clotting blood in its esophagus.
Clotted blood blocks its esophagus
Correct: bacterial coagulase causes blood clotting that blocks the flea's esophagus, so the flea becomes ravenous and tries to bite more hosts.
Endotoxin raises its body heat
Endotoxin is not what changes the flea's behavior; coagulase clots blood that blocks its esophagus, so it keeps biting.
Bacteria digest its blood meal
The bacteria replicate in the gut, but the hunger comes from coagulase clotting the blood and blocking the esophagus.
set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 83 and 81

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How do the salmonelloses other than typhoid fever compare with typhoid fever?
opts: Less severe but more prevalent
Correct: salmonelloses other than typhoid fever (enteric fevers, Salmonella food poisoning and gastroenteritis) are usually less severe than typhoid fever but more prevalent.
More severe and more prevalent
They are more prevalent but usually LESS severe than typhoid fever, the most serious Salmonella disease.
Less severe and less prevalent
They are usually less severe, but MORE prevalent than typhoid fever, not less.
More severe but less prevalent
Both directions are reversed: the animal salmonelloses are usually less severe than typhoid fever but more prevalent.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli is the leading cause of which illness?
opts: Wasting infantile diarrhea
The wasting form of infantile diarrhea is caused by enteropathogenic Escherichia coli; the enterotoxigenic strain causes traveler's diarrhea.
Hemolytic uremic syndrome
Hemolytic uremic syndrome is the kidney complication of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7; the enterotoxigenic strain causes traveler's diarrhea.
Bacillary dysentery
Bacillary dysentery is shigellosis, an invasive disease of the large intestine; the enterotoxigenic strain causes traveler's diarrhea.

Correct: enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli accounts for most cases of traveler's diarrhea: watery diarrhea, cramping and a low-grade to no fever.

Flea bites spread plague; Pasteurella multocida enters through animal bites or scratches.

Cooling-tower aerosols spread Legionella; Pasteurella multocida enters through animal bites or scratches.

Undercooked beef spreads Escherichia coli O157:H7; Pasteurella multocida enters through animal bites or scratches.

set2.q: How does Yersinia pseudotuberculosis infection differ from Yersinia enterocolitica infection?
opts: It causes bloody dysentery
Bloody dysentery is shigellosis; Yersinia pseudotuberculosis resembles Yersinia enterocolitica with more lymph node inflammation.
More lymph node inflammation
Correct: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis causes an infection similar to Yersinia enterocolitica, with more lymph node inflammation; treatment is mostly supportive.
It is spread by fleas
Flea transmission belongs to the nonenteric Yersinia pestis; Yersinia pseudotuberculosis is an enteric with more lymph node inflammation.

set2.q: Why can tularemia relapse?
opts: Its vaccine immunity wanes
Waning vaccine immunity is the pattern behind rising pertussis; tularemia relapses because Francisella persists inside cells.
It hides in the gallbladder
Gallbladder carriage is how chronic typhoid carriers shed Salmonella typhi; tularemia relapses because Francisella persists inside cells.
It persists inside host cells
Correct: the intracellular persistence of Francisella tularensis can lead to relapse.
Its spores survive in the soil
Francisella forms no spores, like the other aerobic nonenteric bacilli; relapse comes from its intracellular persistence.

set2.q: What is the bubo of bubonic plague?
opts: A pus-filled lung cavity
Plague in the lungs is the pneumonic form, spread by aerosol; the bubo is a swollen, necrotic lymph node.
A swollen, necrotic lymph node
Correct: the bacillus multiplies in the flea bite, enters the lymph and causes necrosis and swelling of a node, the bubo, in the groin or axilla.
A gangrenous patch of skin
Purpura that degenerates into necrosis and gangrene is septicemic plague; the bubo is a swollen, necrotic lymph node.
An ulcer at the bite site
An ulcerative skin lesion is a tularemia sign; the plague bubo is a swollen lymph node in the groin or axilla.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Through which kind of host receptor does lipopolysaccharide signal the innate immune system?
opts: A Toll-like receptor
Correct: lipopolysaccharide antigens belong to innate (nonspecific) immunity and interact with host cells through a lipopolysaccharide binding complex and a Toll-like receptor for signaling.
The T-cell receptor
The T-cell receptor belongs to specific, adaptive immunity; lipopolysaccharide is an innate antigen that signals through a Toll-like receptor.
An immunoglobulin E receptor
Immunoglobulin E receptors arm mast cells in allergy; lipopolysaccharide signals the innate system through a binding complex and a Toll-like receptor.
The B-cell receptor
The B-cell receptor is antibody on a B cell, part of the specific response; lipopolysaccharide is sensed innately, through a Toll-like receptor.

set2.q: What divides the Enterobacteriaceae into coliforms and non-coliforms?
opts: Nitrate reduction
All enterics reduce nitrates to nitrites; the coliform split rests on lactose fermentation.
Lactose fermentation
Correct: the enterics are divided into coliforms, the lactose fermenters, and non-coliforms, the non-lactose fermenters.
Oxidase activity
All enterics are oxidase negative, so oxidase does not divide them; lactose fermentation does.
Glucose fermentation
All enterics ferment glucose, so it cannot divide them; coliforms are the lactose fermenters.

mis.Glucose fermentation: shared trait taken for a dividing one
mis.Nitrate reduction: shared trait taken for a dividing one

set2.q: The capsule stain shows rods ringed by large capsules, from a patient with nosocomial pneumonia. Which coliform is it?

Correct: Klebsiella pneumoniae has a large capsule, shown by a capsule stain, and is a cause of nosocomial pneumonia; it is a normal inhabitant of the respiratory tract.

Cattle and pigs

Rodents and their fleas

set2.q: Which Bordetella pertussis adhesion protein, long a vaccine component, is missing from newly developing strains?
opts: Pertactin

Correct: pertactin assists the adhesion of the pertussis bacterium to airway linings and has been a component of vaccines; pertactin-negative strains are developing, a possible connection to the rise of pertussis.
Exotoxin A
Exotoxin A is the Pseudomonas aeruginosa toxin that inhibits protein synthesis; the pertussis adhesion protein in vaccines is pertactin.
Porin OprH
OprH is a Pseudomonas aeruginosa porin membrane protein in a candidate Pseudomonas vaccine; the pertussis adhesion protein is pertactin.
Shiga toxin
Shiga toxin belongs to Shigella and enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli; the pertussis adhesion protein is pertactin.

set2.q: Which condition is related to Proteus infection?
opts: Wasting infantile diarrhea
The wasting form of infantile diarrhea is enteropathogenic Escherichia coli; Proteus is related to bladder and kidney stones.
Ileitis mimicking appendicitis
Inflammation of the ileum that mimics appendicitis is Yersinia enterocolitica; Proteus is related to bladder and kidney stones.
Bladder and kidney stones

Correct: Proteus, an opportunist causing urinary tract and wound infections, pneumonia, septicemia and infant diarrhea, is related to the development of bladder and kidney stones and associated with Crohn's disease.
Hemolytic uremic syndrome
Hemolytic uremic syndrome is the kidney complication of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli; Proteus is related to bladder and kidney stones.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Why do Escherichia coli O157:H7 colonies look black on Rainbow agar?
opts: It makes a black pigment
The black comes from a chromogenic substrate in the agar, not a pigment the bacterium makes; O157:H7 is glucuronidase negative.
It produces hydrogen sulfide
Hydrogen sulfide is a branch of the biochemical tree (Proteus is positive), not the basis of Rainbow agar; O157:H7 is glucuronidase negative.
It lacks glucuronidase
Correct: Rainbow agar carries chromogenic substrates for beta-galactosidase (blue/black) and beta-glucuronidase (red); O157:H7 is glucuronidase negative, so its colonies are black.
It lacks galactosidase
Beta-galactosidase gives the blue-black color, so lacking it would not make colonies black; O157:H7 is glucuronidase negative.

mis.It makes a black pigment: medium color confused with a bacterial pigment

set2.q: Which two illnesses does Legionella cause?
opts: Undulant fever and Malta fever
Undulant fever and Malta fever are both names for brucellosis; Legionella causes Legionnaires disease and Pontiac fever.
Swimmer's ear and corneal ulcers
Swimmer's ear and corneal ulcers are Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in healthy people; Legionella causes Legionnaires disease and Pontiac fever.
Conjunctivitis and chancroid
Conjunctivitis and chancroid are caused by Haemophilus aegyptius and Haemophilus ducreyi; Legionella causes Legionnaires disease and Pontiac fever.
Legionnaires disease, Pontiac fever
Correct: legionellosis takes two forms, Legionnaires disease and Pontiac fever, with fever, cough, diarrhea, abdominal pain and pneumonia.
